name: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc.

profile.description: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc., based in Franklin, Tennessee, operates US behavioral health facilities including acute inpatient psychiatric hospitals, specialty treatment facilities, residential treatment centers and comprehensive treatment centers for opioid use disorder. Q2 2026 revenue was $865.8M, about flat YoY, and adjusted EBITDA fell to $149.2M from $201.8M on higher professional and general liability costs; full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $3.40-3.45B revenue and $590-615M adjusted EBITDA. The company faces a DOJ Criminal Division and SEC investigation into admissions, length of stay and billing, plus securities litigation that followed a 2024 New York Times investigation. Debbie Osteen has returned as CEO. Market cap approximately $2.8B at $29.96.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Acadia's growth over the past five years has come from adding beds and treatment centers within the same model, lifting revenue from $2.09B in 2020 to $3.31B in 2025 without a new business line [1][6]. AI Deployment (1/2): Management says it is in the early stages of using AI in revenue cycle management to analyze data and streamline processes, with no savings quantified [2]. Market Share (1/2): Acadia is a significant national behavioral health operator, but same-facility patient days grew only 0.8% in Q2 2026, which does not show share gains [1]. Product Pipeline (1/2): 2026 capex guidance of $235-255M funds facility expansion, but no specific new service lines with revenue targets were disclosed [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Acadia reports no R&D spending [6].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Acadia's mission of providing compassionate, high-quality behavioral health care identifies whom it serves, but federal investigations and lawsuits over patient detention practices call into question how well that mission is lived [3]. Community Impact (0/2): No distinctive community program with dollar amounts was found. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data was found, and frontline turnover is cited as a cultural issue [2]. Insider Buying (1/2): FMP shows no open-market insider purchases or sales over the last four quarters, only equity grants and small tax-withholding dispositions [7].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically using the Growth weighting (10 weight units). Forward P/E of 16.2 scores 1.0, the provider-reported PEG of 1.37 scores 0.82 at 2x, and the 5-year revenue CAGR of 9.7% (FMP revenue of $2.090B in 2020, continuing operations, to $3.313B in 2025) scores 0.98 at 2x [6][8]. Debt-to-equity of 118% scores 0.79 and revenue growth of -0.4% YoY scores 0.65 [8]. ROE of -41.4% (0.0 at 2x) and profit margin of -33.4% (0.0) reflect the FY2025 net loss of $1.10B, driven largely by non-operating charges [6][8]. Weighted sum 6.03 / 10, rounded to 6. Total debt of $2.59B against $171M cash and negative free cash flow of -$105M are the main balance-sheet concerns [8]. Liquidity floor cleared: 1.62M avg daily volume x $29.96 = about $48.5M.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Acadia provides licensed, in-person acute psychiatric and opioid-treatment care in physical facilities, which AI cannot replace; patient days, not software, drive revenue [1]. Digital mental-health tools could compete at the outpatient margin, but Acadia's acute inpatient and medication-assisted treatment are structurally protected. AI Opportunity (0/1): AI use is limited to early revenue-cycle experiments with no AI revenue [2].

infinite_game.summary: Acadia serves a real and growing need, but recent years show a company in crisis management rather than playing a long game. Allegations that patients were held longer than medically necessary to maximize reimbursement, now under DOJ and SEC investigation, are exactly the finite-game behavior Sinek warns about, though the company denies them. A brief CEO tenure followed by the return of the prior CEO, activist pressure on the board, and frontline turnover all point to low trust and instability.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): Expanding access to behavioral health care is a worthy cause, but the federal investigation into admissions, length of stay and billing suggests it has not consistently governed decisions [3].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): Frontline turnover and inconsistent processes are described as leadership and culture problems, and the new CEO talks about rebuilding a 'culture of urgency' [2]. Leadership has been unstable: Christopher Hunter's short tenure as CEO was followed by Debbie Osteen's return [2].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No management commentary was found acknowledging competitors' strengths or describing learning from peers; the strategic focus is internal stabilization [2].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Acadia's FY2020 results show large discontinued operations from its exit from UK operations, refocusing on US behavioral health [6]. That was a portfolio restructuring, not a reinvention of the business model.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (0/2): Recent decisions have been defensive, focused on stability, staffing and responding to investigations and activist criticism of board governance [2][3]. No example was found of leadership giving up near-term earnings for long-term capability.

investment_thesis: Acadia is a stabilization story in a sector with lasting demand. Q2 2026 beat consensus (adjusted EPS of $0.38 versus $0.33 expected, revenue of $865.8M versus $844.8M expected), and management raised full-year guidance to $3.40-3.45B revenue and $590-615M adjusted EBITDA [1][4]. Excluding the timing of state supplemental payments, same-facility revenue would have grown 3.2% [1]. At a forward P/E of 16.2 on forward EPS of $1.85, up from a 52-week low of $11.43, any clean resolution of the federal investigation could lift the valuation further [8].
thesis_continued: The bear case is legal and reputational overhang plus leverage. The DOJ Criminal Division re-issued subpoenas in December 2024 on admissions, length of stay and billing, the SEC is also involved, and the internal investigation has reached no conclusions [3]. A securities class action covering February 2020 to September 2024 followed a New York Times investigation that hurt patient volumes [5], and patient-safety lawsuits and a CMS immediate-jeopardy citation at a youth hospital add risk [3]. Professional and general liability costs rose $39.3M in Q2 alone, adjusted EBITDA fell 26% YoY, and $2.59B of debt sits against $171M of cash with negative free cash flow [1][8].
key_catalysts: Resolution or narrowing of the DOJ Criminal Division and SEC investigations into admissions and billing practices [3]
Same-facility growth returning to about 3% as state supplemental payment timing normalizes [1]
Delivering on the raised 2026 guidance of $590-615M adjusted EBITDA and $1.45-1.60 adjusted EPS [1]
key_risks: Federal criminal and SEC investigation into length of stay and billing, plus securities class action and derivative suits, could lead to large penalties or Medicaid/Medicare consequences [3]
Rising professional and general liability costs ($39.3M increase in Q2 2026, including a $28.6M reserve adjustment) compressing margins [1]
Leverage of $2.59B debt with negative free cash flow and heavy reliance on Medicaid and state supplemental payments [1][8]
